title: AI and the global economy: implications for central banks (BIS Bulletin No 130)
date_evidence: BIS Bulletin No 130 AI and the global economy: implications for central banks Iñaki Aldasoro, Leonardo Gambacorta, Enisse Kharroubi and Matthias Rottner 28 July 2026
key_claim: AI-related spending on data centres, semiconductors and related infrastructure has reached around 1% of GDP in the most exposed economies; the boom moves demand and supply simultaneously, blurs cyclical signals, shifts national income away from real GDP for upstream exporters, and alters the unobservable benchmarks (natural rates of interest and unemployment) used in monetary policy analysis.
frame_summary: The BIS argues that AI has become macroeconomically large enough to be a first-order problem for monetary policy calibration, because it lifts demand and promises supply at the same time, leaving central banks unable to tell a temporary investment boom from a durable rise in potential output.
verbatim_quote: First, AI is driving a large investment and financing impulse: spending on data centres, semiconductors and related infrastructure has reached around 1% of GDP in the most exposed economies, and the associated capital expenditures increasingly rely on public debt markets as well as private credit.
verbatim_list: By simultaneously affecting demand and supply, AI blurs cyclical signals, complicating central banks' assessment of underlying economic conditions and monetary policy calibration.

in the United States and Australia, where more granular investment data are available, estimated spending on data centres (including the IT equipment they house) and IT manufacturing facilities rose steeply to 0.8% and over 1% of GDP, respectively (purple and brown lines, right-hand scale).
This has caused national income and purchasing power to increase by substantially more than real GDP, which measures production volumes.
These gains have, however, been narrowly concentrated. In Korea, for example, five firms accounted for 43% of export earnings in the first quarter of 2026, up from 27% two years earlier.
Countries with a high AIPI score saw unemployment rates increase by 0.75 percentage points on average between 2023 and 2025; those with low AIPI scores saw flat unemployment rates (Graph 4.C).
The AI boom may thus alter key unobservable benchmarks, including the natural rates of interest and unemployment, frequently used in monetary policy analysis.

Strong activity may reflect temporary demand factors (eg investment booms and wealth effects) rather than sustained increases in potential output, while productivity gains are uneven and hard to measure.

title: Where Is AI in GDP Statistics? Filling the Measurement Gap (Policy Brief 26-7)
key_claim: Deflating the AI portion of the US economy with a quality-adjusted AI price index rather than the conventional deflator would have raised measured real US GDP growth by roughly 2 percentage points in 2024 and roughly 4 percentage points in 2025, presented by the authors as an upper bound.
frame_summary: Korinek and McKelvey argue that the national accounts structurally cannot see the AI sector, and that this measurement gap will become a policy gap because output gaps, productivity and the natural rate of interest are all inferred from accounts that are blind to it, so AI satellite accounts should be built now while the sector is still nominally small.
verbatim_quote: The answer is that real GDP growth would have come in higher by roughly 2 percentage points in 2024 and roughly 4 percentage points in 2025. We present this as an upper bound rather than a point estimate, for two reasons.
verbatim_list: Second, economic policymakers shape policy on the basis of measured output gaps, productivity, and the natural rate of interest, all inferred from national accounts that struggle to see the AI sector.
Our argument here is not that AI mismeasurement today is large enough to materially shift headline numbers but that it may become so within a small number of years.

Byrne, Oliner, and Sichel (2018) found that even within the familiar semiconductor sector, official deflators substantially understated the pace of quality-adjusted price decline; the AI case may pose the same challenge in a more acute form.
notes: URL is the PDF of Policy Brief 26-7; the date_evidence snippet was captured from the publisher's own landing page for this exact PDF (https://www.piie.com/publications/policy-briefs/2026/where-ai-gdp-statistics), which was also fetched and read. The PDF header itself reads only 'PB 26-7 | MAY 2026'. Disclosure: lead author Anton Korinek has headed Transformative AI Economic Studies at the Anthropic Institute since 5 May 2026; co-author Patrick McKelvey is at the Bank of Canada; the brief carries a disclaimer that the views are not those of either institution or PIIE. This source cuts both ways and is used for both the deflator mechanism and the counter-argument. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.

title: World Economic Outlook Update, July 2026: Global Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology
key_claim: The four largest net exporters of AI-related hardware beat first-quarter 2026 growth forecasts by an average of 4.4 percentage points while the rest of the world came in 0.3 percentage point below forecast, with Korea growing 7.5 percent against the 1.8 percent projected in April.
frame_summary: The IMF argues that a single technology cycle has become the dominant sorting variable across countries, so global aggregates now conceal a widening split between economies inside the AI value chain and those outside it, and that policymakers should treat the resulting windfalls as cyclical rather than permanent.
verbatim_quote: For instance, the top four net exporters of AI-related hardware (Taiwan Province of China, Korea, Thailand, and Malaysia) had an average seasonally adjusted annualized surprise of 4.4 percentage points, whereas the surprise for the world's remaining countries was –0.3 percentage point.
verbatim_list: Korea, despite its heavy reliance on imported energy from the Middle East, surprised with a 7.5 percent growth rate, more than four times the 1.8 percent projected in April, powered primarily by a semiconductor and AI-hardware export boom.
If higher inflation is paired with higher demand pressures from the technology-led upturn, central banks may need to do more to avoid overheating.

Economies benefiting from commodity windfalls and the upturn in the global technology cycle should avoid procyclical spending and save or redeploy gains within a credible medium-term fiscal framework anchored in debt sustainability.

publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: The AI Buildout and the Economy: Publicly Available Data to Assess AI's Impact (FEDS Notes)
date_evidence: Soto, Paul E., Mason Thieu, and Jeffrey S. Allen (2026). "The AI Buildout and the Economy: Publicly Available Data to Assess AI's Impact," FEDS Notes. Washington: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, July 17, 2026, https://doi.org/10.17016/2380-7172.4119.
key_claim: AI-related components have contributed meaningfully to quarterly US GDP growth since 2025, but the net contribution is far smaller and more volatile than gross investment implies because the drag from net imports of computers, peripherals and parts offsets much of it, and labour productivity trends across high, medium and low AI-exposure sectors have been relatively consistent over time.
frame_summary: Three Federal Reserve staff economists argue that the AI buildout is already trackable in near-real time with existing public statistics, and that the honest reading of that evidence is a buildout phase rather than a broad-based macroeconomic transformation.
verbatim_quote: From 2025 through the first quarter of 2026, the proposed set of AI-related components have contributed meaningfully to quarterly GDP growth, with software and computer and peripheral equipment the largest positive contributors. The net effect (black line) varies considerably across quarters, as the drag from net exports of computer, peripherals, and parts offsets much of the gross investment in quarters where imports rose sharply.
verbatim_list: While sectors with more exposure appear to have higher labor productivity growth, we see that productivity trends across all three levels have been relatively consistent over time, suggestive of micro-level productivity gains not adding up in aggregate.
Overall, the evidence as of the publication of this note is consistent with a buildout phase rather than the onset of broad-based displacement.

Korean semiconductor export prices (Figure 3) serve as a useful proxy for such input costs, given that Samsung and SK Hynix account for roughly 70 percent of global DRAM supply and are the dominant share for high-bandwidth memory production.
notes: Primary counter-evidence source. Distinct from the earlier April 2026 FEDS Note on AI adoption monitoring by Jeffrey S. Allen. The note is genuinely mixed rather than dismissive: it concedes there is no dedicated national-accounts line item for AI investment and that the equipment has high import content. Standard FEDS Notes disclaimer applies. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.

title: AI and monetary policy: dinner speech by Philip R. Lane at the closing conference of the ESCB ChaMP Research Network
key_claim: The ECB's Executive Board holds that the AI transition pushes the natural rate of interest in both directions at once, through higher investment and lower saving on one side and precautionary uncertainty about the distribution of income gains on the other, leaving the net effect on R* uncertain.
frame_summary: Lane argues that AI is not a clean supply shock for monetary policy but a source of two-sided uncertainty about the anchors of policy themselves, so central banks should treat R* and potential output as contested estimates during the transition rather than as fixed reference points.
verbatim_quote: Given these different mechanisms, the net effect of the AI transition on R* remains uncertain.
verbatim_list: In one direction, sustained optimism about the income and productivity gains from AI would boost investment and reduce savings, putting upward pressure on R*. In the opposite direction, the more households and firms are uncertain about the trajectory of the AI-induced income path and the distribution of income gains across regions and income groups, the less an increase in R* would materialise.
notes: Delivered on Lane's behalf by Philipp Hartmann, Deputy Director General Economics, per footnote 1. The speech cross-references the BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 in footnote 2. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.

title: The AI boom has doubled computing infrastructure's share of US GDP
date_evidence: Data Insight Jun. 5, 2026 # The AI boom has doubled computing infrastructure's share of US GDP
key_claim: AI-related data centre construction, compute hardware and networking accounted for about 0.8% of US GDP in Q1 2026, taking computing infrastructure as a whole to about 1.5% of GDP against a 2015-2022 average of about 0.7%, and all of these figures are nominal.
frame_summary: Epoch AI argues that the data-centre buildout, while still a small share of GDP in absolute terms, has doubled computing infrastructure's weight in the US economy and become the leading driver of growth in private investment, and it flags that the nominal figures understate real compute growth because of quality improvement.
verbatim_quote: Investment in AI-related data center construction, compute hardware, and networking equipment accounted for ~0.8% of US GDP in Q1 2026, driving computing infrastructure as a whole to ~1.5% of GDP, up from a 2015–2022 average of ~0.7%.
verbatim_list: All figures are nominal. Real C&P growth is larger than nominal growth due to quality improvements in chips and servers, while data center construction cost inflation makes real construction growth slower than nominal.
AI infrastructure is now the leading driver of growth in private investment in the US.
notes: Author Isabel Juniewicz. Also serves as partial counter-evidence: the page's own headline framing on the site index is that the buildout share of US GDP 'is still relatively small (but rapidly growing)'. The dash in '2015–2022' is an en dash (U+2013), reproduced as printed. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.

title: Large Firms With at Least 20 Employees Biggest AI Users (Business Trends and Outlook Survey)
key_claim: Business Trends and Outlook Survey data for December 2025 to May 2026 show overall US business AI use hovering between 17% and 20%, with a national rate of 19.8% as of 3 May 2026 against 39.7% in Information and 33.9% in Finance and Insurance.
frame_summary: The Census Bureau argues that AI use in the US business population is growing but remains concentrated in larger firms and a handful of sectors, so headline adoption is not evidence of economy-wide diffusion.
verbatim_quote: As of May 3, 2026, the AI use rates in the Information (39.7%) and Finance and Insurance (33.9%) sectors were both higher than the national rate (19.8%) but neither reported significant shifts since December.
verbatim_list: The BTOS data (December 2025 to May 2026) show that overall AI usage hovered between 17% and 20% — and that between 20% and 23% of businesses expected to be using it in the next six months.
notes: Authors Adam Grundy, Cory Breaux and Dhanapati Khatiwoda. The verbatim quote is reproduced with the two inline hyperlinks (on 'Information' and 'Finance and Insurance') stripped, as rendered text. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.

title: The central bank of central banks just released its flagship annual report and it sees a $1 trillion AI investment boom headed for a reckoning
key_claim: The five largest hyperscalers are on pace to spend more than $1 trillion on AI-related capital expenditure across 2025 and 2026 combined, a sum the BIS says already outpaces their earnings and free cash flow.
frame_summary: Fortune argues that the BIS has placed the AI capex cycle in the lineage of canal mania, the railway bubble and the dot-com crash, and that the danger lies less in the scale of the spending than in how it is financed.
verbatim_quote: The five largest hyperscalers are on pace to spend more than $1 trillion on AI-related capital expenditure across 2025 and 2026 combined — a sum the BIS says is already outpacing their earnings and free cash flow, forcing some to issue debt to cover the gap.
verbatim_list: "The scale and pace of the current AI investment boom, accompanied by expectations of large productivity payoffs, bear resemblance to these precedents," the BIS writes in its Annual Economic Report 2026, released Sunday.
notes: Author Nick Lichtenberg, Business Editor. Reporting on the BIS Annual Economic Report 2026, released 28 June 2026.
